title: A repeating failure is a fault to find
statement: A failure that repeats across items or retries is a fault, not noise: redrafting or rescoring won't fix it, so rule out broken measurement, find its cause and test it.
example: Nine targeted fixes, each for one specific fault, added 15.1 points to the pass rate.
detail: At 81.9% the AP question work's remaining failures were systematic, not random (`icloud-work/ML learnings/gemini_benchmark_relentless.md`). Of about 40-50 automated iterations most changed nothing, and the nine that worked each removed a specific code or prompt bug behind a specific failing dimension, adding 15.1 points in about 48 hours. The project's diagnostic method goes from the aggregate to the failing dimension and items, then two or three hypotheses and a test that tells them apart, with a catalogue of signatures: a whole unit failing points to wrong scope labels, a whole item type to missing examples, right content on the wrong topic to an ignored constraint, and wrong specifics to invented details (`icloud-work/ML learnings/debugging_methodology.md`). Each time a step was skipped, going from an aggregate straight to a fix, a training run was wasted. Signs of such a failure include a whole item type at zero or all passing, and scores bunched under the pass line. Rule out a broken measurement as well as a broken pipeline.
against: A repeating failure is not always fixable in the instructions: "The failure is at the weight level, not the prompt level." (`icloud-work/ML learnings/prompt_engineering_deep_dive.md`, line 73), and the same source's last 3% were random slips (`icloud-work/ML learnings/gemini_benchmark_relentless.md`, line 208). A whole item type once failed because of a routing fault, not missing examples (`icloud-work/ML learnings/sft_v7_benchmark_postmortem.md`, line 26), and even with the method the first hypotheses were often wrong (`icloud-work/ML learnings/stage2_postmortem_full.md`, line 180). The none-or-all rule is stated from one incident, not measured across runs: "**NOT re-verified by me on disk this turn; this is the directive's framing, not new measurement.**" (icloud-work/aptraining/workspace/comms/_deprecated/outboxes/from_research/2026-05-01T1300Z_R44_eval_phantom_class.md, 32). The reading of bunched scores rests on one item type in two runs. Inferred from counts: the reports never cross-tabulate rule by item type. In both runs the hard-fail count equals the fill-in count (18 and 16), and the sampled hard-fail examples are all fill-in items. The review's own caveat: drift in the judge over the window can't be fully excluded, so per-version rates should be re-confirmed on one pinned judge version. the 100-draft figure is reasoning from the type of failure, not a measured run. the same project credits a three-attempt retry with a stronger-model fallback, alongside a check before generation, for one question type's rise from 90% to 100% (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/CHANGELOG.md`). The gate that measured the rounds is itself stochastic: boundary items pass one draw and fail a fresh one, about 22% on a second draw, so a single round's rate carries noise (`grade3-reading/artifacts/alpha-read-packager/v2_final_package/docs/COURSE_QUALITY_GATE_REPORT.md`). Among items that failed every scoring, the evidence does not single out near misses: three of the six that scored 0.7-0.8 every time became triple passes once the writer was given each objective's scope limits and sub-objectives, as did both items with zero scores, while two near misses did not move (`project_richer_rag_resolves_stable_fails.md`, lines 27-35). A failure that repeats can be the judge's own: a '0%' on one item type was 9 real verdicts and 91 timeouts (`feedback_ib_grader_v266_dbq_mcqset_timeout_99pct_at_concurrency_default_2026_06_02.md`, line 11). And a structural failure holds for one judge version and one generator: a grounded generator's document sets passed a later judge 139 of 154 times (`recipe_track_b_openstax_pair_generation.md`, line 67). The lifts were scored by the same grader that picked the best version; a held-out judge agreed on 21 of 24 rescued items, so part of the measured lift may be the picking fitting the grader. A flip is not always a slip: a later change to the same evaluator found that the flips it studied were not noise on clean items but genuine defects in the scoring guide that it caught on some runs and missed on others, and fixed them by making that check mandatory.

evidence.quote: At 81.9%, the system was generating correct AP questions most of the time. The remaining ~18% failures were not random — they were systematic, patterned failures. The key insight that drove the relentless push: every failure is evidence of a specific, fixable bug.
**Total:** 15.1 percentage point improvement from 9 targeted fixes over ~48 hours.

The system applied ~40-50 iterations over 48 hours. Most iterations were 0.0% improvement. 9 were significant. The 9 that worked all had the same structure: **a specific, identifiable code/prompt bug causing a specific, measurable dimension to fail.**
**60-80%:** Usually systematic bugs (wrong metadata, wrong course, missing training examples for a type)

**Signature:** Entire unit/course at 0% despite other units passing
**Cause:** Wrong metadata (time period, course, unit) being passed to model

**Signature:** Entire type/class at 0% or near-0%
**Cause:** That class has little or no representation in training data

**Signature:** Model generates correct content for the WRONG thing it was told to do
**Cause:** Training data lacked hard negatives for constraint adherence

**Signature:** Facts are mostly right, but specific details (dates, attributions, names) are wrong
**Cause:** Model's parametric memory generates plausible details that aren't factually correct

4. HYPOTHESIS → generate 2-3 possible root causes
5. DISTINGUISH → find the test that differentiates hypotheses
6. CONFIRM → run the test, accept one hypothesis
Never skip to step 7. Every time we skipped steps (went from aggregate failure to guessing at a fix), we wasted a training run.

**The math matches theory:** If single-shot P=0.89, then N=5 → 1-(1-0.89)^5 = 99.4% theoretical. Actual 98.6% is slightly below theoretical (some questions are systematically hard — Best-of-N can't overcome systematic failures). For our model at P=0.60, N=5 → 1-(0.40)^5 = 99.0% theoretical, practical ~92%.

With Best-of-N=5: generating 5 candidates, evaluating all, picking the best (best scored 0.96). 50% means roughly half the best-of-5 candidates are still failing factual_accuracy hard-fails. The model's parametric knowledge is shaky on Colonial era APUSH specifics.

**Inference-time verification / regeneration:** Per project principles, "verification and regeneration are not valid approaches." Beyond the principle, our evaluator results show the model consistently picks wrong facts — this is a systematic failure, not a stochastic one that retries would fix.

**Practical implication:** If the 14B model's failure rate is 67% (as currently), even N=100 won't reliably get to 90%+ because the *type* of failures (fabricated attribution) is deterministic, not stochastic. But if data quality fixes bring pass rate to 70-80%, then Best-of-N=5 at $0.20/M is more economical than 70B at $0.90/M.
So Best-of-N is a multiplier, not a miracle. The base model still needs to be competent. Target P≥0.60 per type before Best-of-N becomes highly effective.
